rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the passage concerns the sea and its gifts, it places the sea pronoun before the ships' sailing; a passage centered on conveyances instead foregrounds the ships and their state.
rows.anchor: فلما كان الكلام على البحر قدم ضمير البحر على المخر فقال: (وترى الفلك فيه مواخر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isra places “for people” before “in this Quran,” fitting its prior discussion of people and divine favors; Kahf delays it, matching a sūra that opens with the Quran before its human stories.
rows.anchor: قدم (للناس) على (في هذه القرآن) في الإسراء وأخرها في (الكهف)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kufūr means denial of blessings, so Isra's ending fits its preceding mention of divine favor; 76:3 likewise contrasts being thankful with being ungrateful.
rows.anchor: والكُفُور: هو جحد النعم، فناسب ذلك تقدم ذكر النعمة والرحمة والفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kahf's ending about human contentiousness fits its many surrounding disputes: the two companions' dialogue, unbelievers' arguments, Moses' debate, and the instruction not to dispute about the youths.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر قبلها وبعدها من المحاورات والجدل والمراء من مثل قوله تعالى

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqara concerns almsgiving: the donor gives rather than earns, so “thing” precedes “earnings”; Ibrahim concerns deeds, where the worker is an earner, so earnings comes first.
rows.anchor: آية البقرة في سياق الإنفاق والصدقة، والمنفقُ معطٍ وليس كاسباً، ولذلك أَخَّر الكسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Al Imran, consolation after the wounds of Uhud puts hearts before the angelic aid and adds “for you”; in Anfal's fuller account of Badr's victory and divine aid, “by it” comes first.
rows.anchor: ففي آل عمران ذكر معركة بدر تمهيداً لذكر موقعة أُحد وما أصابهم فيها من قرح وحزن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqara's prohibition formula puts “bihi” before “for other than God”; the author sets this ordering against the food-prohibition formulations in Maida and Anam.
rows.anchor: وَمَآ أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ الله} [البقرة: 173] فقدم (به) على (لغير الله)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He glosses mā uhilla bihi as the animal over whose slaughter a voice is raised, identifying it with al-bahīma.
rows.anchor: ومعنى: (ما أهل به) : ما رُفع الصوتُ بذبحهِ وهو البهمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses al-rīḥ for punishment; its sole apparently beneficial occurrence, 10:22, turns into a storm and ends badly.
rows.anchor: ولم يستعمل الريح في الخير إلا في موطن واحد أعقبها بالشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses amṭara for punitive rain but ghayth for good: 42:28 brings mercy after despair, and 12:49 describes a year of relief and harvest.
rows.anchor: لا تجد القرآن يلفظ به إلا في موضع الانتقام بخلاف الغيث الذي يذكره القرآن في الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses al-ʿuyūn only for water springs, while it uses aʿyun for human sight; the author notes ten occurrences of the former usage.
rows.anchor: فلم يستعمل العيون إلا لعيون الماء. وقد وردت كلمة (العيون) في القرآن الكريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses waṣṣā (with gemination) for religious and moral matters, but awṣā for material matters such as inheritance.
rows.anchor: فكل ما ورد فيه من (وصّى) بالتشديد فهو في الدين والأمور المعنوية، وكل ما ورد من (أوصى) فهو في الأمور المادية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sole moral use of awṣā is 19:31, where the instruction joins prayer to zakat, a material obligation.
rows.anchor: ولم ترد (أوصى) في القرآن الكريم للأمور المعنوية إلا في موطن واحد اقترنت فيه بأمر مادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unassimilated form is Hijazi and assimilation Tamimi; the Quran uses the split form when the Messenger is named and the assimilated form when the phrase names God alone, reflecting one versus two.
rows.anchor: الفَكُّ لغةُ الحجاز والإدغام لغة تميم، ولكن القرآن استعملهما استعمالاً خاصاً فحيث ورد ذكر الرسول فك الإدغام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's precise, varied word choices still form an integrated literary whole: each expression fits its local context and harmonizes with its other occurrences.
rows.anchor: ومع هذا الاستعمال الرياضي الإحصائي العجيب للألفاظ فالتعبير القرآني هو في قمة الأدب والفن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The degree of emphasis varies precisely with context: the Quran uses no particle, inna, the lām, or both, and none can be added or removed without disrupting its fit.
rows.anchor: فهو يقول مثلاً: (إن الله شديد العقاب) مؤكداً بإن وحدها في مواطن عديدة من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conditional replies also vary with context: Noah's answer is unreinforced, one reply is emphatic, and another adds both an emphatic answer and the prefatory lām on the condition.
rows.anchor: بتوكيد الجواب وبذكر اللام الموطئة قبل الشرط، كل ذلك حسبما يقتضيه الموطن والسياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran varies interrogative forms—hamza or hal, mā or mādhā—even in the same story, as shown in the question to Abraham's people.
rows.anchor: فهو قد يستفهم مرة بالهمزة ومرة بـ (هل)

words: لَّا يَقْدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَىْءٍۢ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic word order varies with context: it alternates which term comes first in paired expressions, including the order of earnings and “thing,” and of bowing and prostration.
rows.anchor: وقُلْ مثل ذلك عن التقديم والتأخير. فهو قد يُقدِّمُ كلمةً في مكان ويُؤخِّرها في مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A parallel warning omits “nor will He look at them” in Baqara but includes it in Al Imran; the author says such additions and omissions are placed with artistic precision.
rows.anchor: فيزيد عبارة (ولا ينظر إليهم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites 39:23 for the Quran's devotional effect: its repeated, coherent discourse makes reverent believers' skins shiver, then their skins and hearts soften toward God's remembrance.
rows.anchor: تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ الذين يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ إلى ذِكْرِ الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic expression has been studied through its imagery, sound and rhythm, word choice, and the coherence of its sūras, verses, openings, and endings; these studies reveal a tightly connected composition.
rows.anchor: ودُرسَ تناسبُ سورهِ سورةً سورة، وتناسب آياته آية آية، وتناسب فواتح السور وخواتمها

rows.speaker: الفخر الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the Quran is like one sūra because its parts connect to one another, indeed like one verse.
rows.anchor: كما قال الفخر الرازي: إن القرآن كالسورة الواحدة لاتصال بعضه ببعض بل هي كالآية الواحدة
